qs.q: Indoor residual spraying is primarily most effective against insect vectors that exhibit which behavioral trait?
qs.e: Indoor residual spraying targets vectors that rest indoors after feeding, meaning endophilic insects are most susceptible to this control method. Exophilic vectors spend more time outdoors and avoid indoor residues.

qs.q: Indoor residual spraying is most effective against vectors that are:
o: Restricted exclusively to animal blood meals
Endophilic and resting on treated indoor surfaces
Exophilic and resting outdoors after feeding
Active only in open water breeding sites
qs.e: Indoor residual spraying works when vectors rest on insecticide-treated indoor surfaces; therefore it is most useful against endophilic vectors.

qs.q: Indoor residual spraying is BEST effective against insects vectors of pathogens.
qs.e: Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) involves applying insecticides to interior walls and surfaces where vectors rest. It is most effective against endophilic insects that prefer to rest indoors after feeding. Exophagic insects feed outdoors, endophagic insects feed indoors but may rest outdoors, and exophilic insects rest outdoors - all reducing IRS effectiveness. es.q: Explain the principle of indoor residual spraying (IRS) in mosquito control.
es.m:
- A residual insecticide is applied to suitable indoor wall or ceiling surfaces.
- Endophilic mosquitoes resting on treated surfaces may contact the insecticide and die or become less likely to survive.
- High coverage is important for community-level impact.
- Effectiveness depends on mosquito resting behavior, insecticide susceptibility, correct application and sustained program coverage.

ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) applies long‑lasting insecticides to walls where malaria vectors rest, cutting transmission. It complements bed nets and chemoprophylaxis, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: IRS targets endophilic mosquitoes that rest on walls after feeding. By killing them on contact, it reduces human–vector contact and malaria incidence.
b: Applied to interior walls and surfaces

sections.p: Anopheles mosquitoes, the primary malaria vectors, are endophilic and endophagic, making them susceptible to IRS.
Mosquitoes bite humans, ingest parasites, and after a 10‑14 day extrinsic incubation period, become infectious. IRS interrupts this cycle by killing mosquitoes before they can transmit.
Malaria, caused by Plasmodium spp., remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in many low‑resource regions.
b: High mortality in children and pregnant women

sections.p: Clinical suspicion plus rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or microscopy confirm malaria. IRS does not diagnose but reduces prevalence.

t.b: Detects parasites; confirms species and parasitemia level; high specificity
Quick detection of HRP2 or pLDH antigens; useful where microscopy unavailable; may miss low parasitemia

sections.p: IRS is a vector control strategy, not a treatment. It is combined with insecticide‑treated nets and antimalarial drugs for patients.

t.b: Determines if local mosquitoes are susceptible; informs choice of insecticide
Measures % of houses sprayed; low coverage limits impact

sections.p: IRS is most effective against endophilic vectors; its success depends on high coverage and proper application. Resistance surveillance is essential.
b: Resistance to pyrethroids is rising; switch to organophosphates if needed

faq.q: What is the main advantage of IRS over bed nets?
faq.a: IRS kills mosquitoes that rest on walls, reducing overall vector density, while nets only protect individuals during sleep.

faq.q: Can IRS be used in all climates?
faq.a: IRS is effective where vectors rest indoors; in very hot or humid climates, wall adhesion may be reduced, requiring alternative strategies.

faq.q: How often should IRS be repeated?
faq.a: Typically every 6–12 months, depending on insecticide residual life and local transmission intensity.
